Journal of Economic Geography.title: Urban densification to support climate adaptation: balancing costs and agglomeration benefits in the Netherlands
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: Where should we build new housing under growing climate hazards? This study develops a framework that balances the economic benefits of density against the geographically varying costs of climate adaptation. We apply it to the Netherlands, where demand for new housing is high, but much of the land lies in floodplains or subsidence-prone areas. Agglomeration benefits are proxied by land values, while adaptation costs are derived from engineering estimates of flood protection and soil subsidence. Combining these data allows us to map spatial trade-offs and identify where development remains welfare-enhancing. Our findings show that dense cities continue to generate strong net welfare gains, even in places with high costs, while low-density settlements generate a welfare loss for new housing. We identify density thresholds above which housing development becomes feasible. Many medium-sized Dutch cities already exceed these thresholds, making densification more beneficial than peripheral expansion. Climate adaptation thus strengthens—rather than weakens—the case for urban densification.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: Indigenous communities and the shaping of a lithium labour regime in Jujuy’s salt-flat ecologies
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: This article examines how Indigenous communities shape the lithium-mining labour regime in the Atacama Puna of Jujuy, Argentina. Drawing on ethnographic research, it shows how global mining arrangements are territorially reconfigured through communal landownership, community negotiation, subcontracting, salt-flat ecologies and historically constituted forms of social reproduction. These articulations produce distinctive recruitment practices, labour segmentation, uneven occupational risks and gendered reproductive burdens. The article advances labour-regime analysis by demonstrating that communities actively constitute the labour regimes of the energy transition through their political organisation, property relations and livelihood histories within the specific ecological conditions of the salt flats.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: Polycrisis and labour agency in global production networks: evidence from Bangladesh’s apparel industry
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: This article explains how temporally uneven polycrisis reshapes labour agency within apparel production networks. Developing a spatial–temporal analytical framework, it shows how interactions, amplification, and acceleration across crises reconfigure workers’ opportunity structures through legitimacy, profitability, and social reproduction pressures. This qualitative case study of Bangladesh’s apparel industry examines how the Rana Plaza accident, COVID-19, and the climate crisis interacted to produce cumulative effects that enabled openings and constrained mobilization, shifting labour agency across associational, coalitional, and micro-practices over time. The study advances labour regime analysis by demonstrating the temporal contingency and spatial situatedness of labour agency during polycrisis.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: The impact of geographical and technological proximity on knowledge spillovers from formal standards
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: Proximity is traditionally viewed as crucial for overcoming the search and transfer costs associated with imperfectly codified knowledge. But does proximity still matter when formal standard publication jointly enhances the codification, certainty, and accessibility of technical knowledge? Evidence from the U.S. Information and Communication Technology industry shows that technological proximity drives substantial spillover gains, largely irrespective of location. Conversely, geographical proximity confers a compensating advantage when technological proximity is low. We reveal a nuanced interplay of proximity in knowledge spillovers: while formal standardization effectively flattens the world for the technologically proximate, co-location remains vital for their less proximate counterparts.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: Peripheral participation, metropolitan ownership: core and periphery configurations in Japan’s Green Transformation technological paths
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: Research on innovation beyond metropolitan cores has paid less attention to whether peripheral participation is matched by formal ownership of patents on key technological paths. We distinguish spatial and network participation from the headquarters geography of patent applicants, and apply kernel density, core–periphery network, and main-path analyses to sixty-two Japanese Green Transformation technologies. Four technology participation configurations emerge. Yet most main-path patent–firm links involve firms headquartered in Japan’s three major metropolitan areas. The study highlights that participation in main technological paths differs from ownership, which marks the tensions between core and peripheral configurations of inventive activity.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: People, places, and firms: improving our understanding of wage and productivity disparities
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: In many countries spatial disparities in wages and productivity are large and persistent. This raises questions about the causes and consequences of such disparities. Two inter-related issues—the sorting of high skilled workers and the productivity benefits of urban density—are central to the way in which urban economists have approached these questions. In this commentary, we argue that despite the emerging consensus that sorting matters for wage disparities, the literature has made less progress on other dimensions of these disparities and a number of methodological issues remain unresolved.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: Being(s) there(s)—geographies of tacit knowledge through avatars, telepresence robots, and holograms
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: We aim to understand emerging geographies of tacit knowledge through advanced remote-work technologies: telepresence robots, holograms and virtual avatars. These technologies enable ‘being there’ in more than one location (and space) at once and using communication that resembles a face-to-face experience. We examine, if tacit knowledge can be shared through these technologies. Based on interviews and autoethnography, we find that each technology confers the ability to exert specific spatial agency elsewhere. From the intellectualist perspective, all studied technologies allow the sharing of some tacit knowledge, whereas virtual avatars enable the sharing of some tacit knowledge also from the phenomenological perspective.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: Building without income mixing: public housing quotas in France
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: We study the effects of the SRU law introduced in France in December 2000 to support scattered development of public housing in cities and favor social mixity. This law imposes 20 per cent of public dwellings to all medium and large municipalities of large-enough cities, with fees for those not abiding by the law. Using exhaustive fiscal data, we evaluate the effects of the law over the 1996–2008 period using a difference-in-differences approach at the municipality and neighborhood levels. We find that the law stimulated public housing construction in treated municipalities, but only slightly increased the presence of low-income households. Indeed, new public dwellings enter categories to which medium-income are eligible and most additional occupants are not poor. Within municipalities, the policy decreased public housing segregation but it barely decreased low-income segregation. This comes from local authorities increasing over time the presence of public dwellings in neighborhoods away from existing public housing but in places concentrating low-income households.

Journal of Economic Geography.title: Polycrisis and global production networks: a framework for understanding industry dynamics in times of accumulated uncertainty
Journal of Economic Geography.abstract: Global production networks (GPNs) are currently impacted by multiple crises. Yet, crises have received little attention in GPN scholarship. This article shows how the entangled drivers of polycrisis affect the economic geographies of suppliers and their integration into GPNs. It develops an analytical framework for exploration of accumulated uncertainties in conjunctural moments of polycrisis. The management of unknown ‘uncertainties’ other than ‘risk’ for lead firms is a key element. Focusing on Bangladesh’s apparel industry, this article explores the industry’s responses and struggles, and provides insights into the wider processes of inclusion and exclusion in the global economy during polycrisis.

Urban Studies.title: The rubble and beyond: Expanding urbicide through affective geographies and the settler-colonial longue durée
Urban Studies.abstract: Urbicide scholarship has established, in varying ways, that ‘killing a city’ reaches beyond the material. Yet the concepts used to name this ‘reach’ do not describe the same object or make the same analytical claim. The question is therefore not only whether urbicide reaches beyond the material, but what a given conceptualisation allows us to understand about what destruction reaches. This article expands urbicide scholarship by theorising affect not as an additional dimension or effect of destruction, but as a capacity enabled by material and human–nonhuman relations through which violence can be reached. The argument is developed through a situated reading of contemporary urbicidal violence in Gaza (2023–ongoing), where recurrent military operations have compounded destruction while foreclosing reconstruction between them, within a longer settler-colonial history of displacement and enclosure. Drawing on Anderson’s account of morale and affective geographies literature, the article shows how destruction reaches the material and relational conditions through which affective capacities are constituted and exercised. It further proposes storytelling and counter-mapping as situated forms of evidence for tracing the reach of this destruction: memories, attachments, spatial knowledge and relations that conventional damage assessment cannot capture. Locating these processes within the settler-colonial longue durée expands the concept of urbicide showing how its reach is shaped by historically specific conditions of enclosure, cumulative destruction and the absence of a stable aftermath.

Urban Studies.title: Each building tells a story: A New York City neighborhood on the cusp of densification
Urban Studies.abstract: This study seeks to understand the business of densification through analysis of public policies, property records, and “the everyday” in a rapidly changing Manhattan neighborhood. Our case study of Inwood uses a new conceptual framework for urban policy analysis to bring multiple data sources together to examine four sites that show how key elements of New York City’s rezoning strategy intersects with other housing policies. Our findings speak to the challenges of maintaining affordable housing stock amid densification and the importance of including everyday experiences in policy analysis. We find that new densification policies interact with pre-existing policies to produce complex, contradictory outcomes. For example, de-densification coexists with densification. Second, although some manifestations of densification are visible, such as high-rise buildings, others are not, including tenant displacement and apartment warehousing. Finally, we find that policy implementation works as ad hoc policy making because actors seek policy changes through alternative channels after rezoning is formally adopted.

Urban Studies.title: Activity spaces, community resource brokers, and real-time stress and affect: Evidence from the Boston Activity Space and Health Study
Urban Studies.abstract: While we know that the places where we live matter for our health and well-being, other spaces in the city we visit during the day—like places where we work, worship, exercise, and buy groceries—also matter. Little work, however, has explored how daily experiences with these routine community institutions and organizations shape our emotional responses. This study uses data from the Boston Activity Space and Health Study (BASHS), a smartphone-based data collection of adults’ GPS locations and ecological momentary assessments, to capture in-the-moment responses to their daily activity space environments for 7 days. We use random effects models to estimate associations between resource broker access and real-time accounts of stress and affect, and whether these relationships are conditional on the utilization of the resource brokers. Our findings suggest that beyond having regular access to community resource brokers, utilizing them on a regular basis is impactful for alleviating momentary emotional and physiological distress. By detailing the unique role of resource brokers, the current study makes substantive and methodological contributions to our understanding of how activity spaces matter for health and well-being.

Urban Studies.title: Planning for circular urban metabolism: Intertwining skills and spatial transformation for manufacturing transition in Padua and Venice, Italy
Urban Studies.abstract: The shift from a linear to a circular economic structure needs a new urban metabolism that minimizes waste and the use of raw materials and energy. However, a city’s potential for circularity is contingent upon its manufacturing path-dependency, both from an economic and spatial perspective. The research looks at two Italian industrial areas—Padua and Venice—and proceeds to investigate the recent dynamics of their manufacturing spatial distribution at the “transect” level scale. Using a mixed-method approach that combines morphological-spatial analysis, urban planning assessment, and quantitative labor and waste data, the study investigates how manufacturing industries contribute to circular transitions and how planning policies can support or hinder this process. Findings show that technological manufacturing, supported by technical skills and green jobs, drives circular performance through waste prevention and recycling. Industrial diversification and firm relatedness further enable symbiotic material flows. However, both cities reveal a persistent misalignment between emerging circular dynamics and existing zoning frameworks. While Padua has begun adopting mixed-use zoning, planning strategies in both areas remain fragmented and reactive. The paper calls for more integrated, circularity-oriented spatial planning that mobilizes skills and proximity as key territorial resources.

Urban Studies.title: Wealth, homeownership, and land use regulatory changes
Urban Studies.abstract: This paper examines patterns of land use regulatory changes in Santiago, Chile, focusing on downzoning (stricter regulations) and upzoning (more flexible regulations), and their associations with sociodemographic factors. We analyze an original georeferenced dataset covering all 34 urban municipalities of Santiago over 20 years, together with 19 semi-structured interviews with key actors. The quantitative analysis suggests that high-income neighborhoods are associated with a greater likelihood of downzoning when homeownership is comparatively low. With our block-level measure of wealth, however, this association is not statistically distinguishable from zero at the sample-average homeownership rate and becomes negative at higher rates. Therefore, in affluent neighborhoods, the significant presence of homeowners is associated with less probability of downzoning. Outside high-income neighborhoods, higher homeownership is instead associated with downzoning. Qualitative evidence points to the growing role of organized residents, with socially connected groups using participatory reforms and informal ties to municipal decision-makers to shape local regulatory debates. This positive association is absent when the analysis is restricted to large-scale zoning changes. The findings contribute to debates between the “growth machine” and “homevoter” theories by suggesting that the relevance of each framework may vary across patterns of social segmentation and local demographic structures.

Urban Studies.title: The gendered right to the city: Mediated access, urban agriculture and women’s empowerment in Kumasi
Urban Studies.abstract: Urban space is a vital resource for city dwellers. While literature examines the use of formal public spaces by urban residents for commerce and social activities, scholarly attention to informal agricultural spaces remains limited. This study uses a synthesis of Kabeer’s empowerment framework and Lefebvre’s right to the city to analyse women’s access to and use of urban space for agriculture in Ghana as a transformative space where gender, body and empowerment intersect. Our findings reveal that male networks serve as gatekeepers through whom women access urban space for urban agriculture. While women’s access to this social capital is empowering, it indicates that women’s right to the city and to spatial justice is mediated, achieved through relational networks and experienced as a relational right. Our findings further reveal that women appropriate these urban spaces in ways that enhance their general well-being, bodily sovereignty and promote intergenerational rights to the city for their children. By demonstrating how women’s spatial access enables agency, bodily sovereignty and the pursuit of intergenerational rights, we argue for a more nuanced understanding of empowerment and rights within informal urban contexts in the Global South.

Urban Studies.title: Limits on growth: Governing urban futures in Beijing
Urban Studies.abstract: This paper conceptualises limits on growth in Beijing, whose 2016–2035 master plan constructs a highly selective national capital for the central state by removing functions and populations deemed non-essential. Drawing on archival analysis of planning documents since 1949, extensive expert and ethnographic interviews, and multi-sited fieldwork conducted between 2017 and 2023, it develops a Lefebvrian spatio-temporal framework with three relational dimensions for analysing urban future-making. Temporal entanglements show how a historically sedimented anti-metropolis disposition is reactivated amid contemporary state recentralisation. Performative governance examines how the diagnosis of ‘big city disease’ reframes demographic and functional pressures as urban pathology, legitimising relocation and greening as therapeutic intervention. Lived futurity reveals how officials, villagers and migrants negotiate these measures through procrastination, speculation and retreat. The article theorises limits on growth as an emergent mode of Chinese statecraft in which extra-economic priorities selectively guide the production of the urban future. Situating Beijing within a wider, politically heterogeneous turn that increasingly treats demographic and territorial growth as a crisis, it reconceives urban future-making as a politics of foreclosure: not only who profits from growth, but who is permitted to remain when growth is limited by design.

Urban Studies.title: The simultaneous slow death and persistent vitality of social infrastructure in elite neighbourhoods
Urban Studies.abstract: This article examines the vitality of social life at street level over time in the patrician elite area of Kensington, London. We consider how luxury amenities, prime homes and high-end stores intersect with the durable presence of an everyday, working city comprising diverse social infrastructures: budget hotels, rent-controlled housing and interstitial social spaces of cafes, parks and street benches. These layers of uses and users co-exist in complex time–space configurations despite the historical and contemporary designation of the neighbourhood as an elite space. Using a range of data sources, we show how the neighbourhood contains distinct features that enable the limited and partial social engagement and hypermobility of wealthy bodies with the social life of the area. However, we also find a diverse social history, culture and complex grounded experiences at street level involving a wide range of residents and other users. These observations demonstrate how, even in the most elite of urban neighbourhoods, spaces remain socially complex and diverse, despite ongoing tensions.

Urban Studies.title: Narrating ontologies of ruination in the disciplinary blur: Ruins as temporal gardens, trees as legal witnesses and birds as world-makers
Urban Studies.abstract: This commentary investigates the disciplinary blur that challenges the dual ontology of ruination as being both an urban/architectural transformation and an ecological phenomenon. It defies categorizations of objective knowledge and comes to terms with multispecies and interdisciplinary approaches, both historiographically and ethnographically, readjusting to the multiple temporalities of the nonhuman world-making projects that the human-made ruin becomes part of. Drawing on the urban ruin of 19 th -century Manchester (Cottonopolis), England, and the architectural ruins of contemporary Mogador, Morocco, it argues that the temporalities of the nonhuman, intersected respectively with periodicities of industrial contamination and human abandonment, transform the singular obsolete narrative of ruins into a plural transdisciplinary debate questioning the unyielding becoming of urban space. The text’s historiographical and ethnographical micronarratives, woven together through storytelling, theorize the transformative temporalities of urban nature and their capacity to provide the anthropogenic ruin with a collaborative ecological agency. This, the commentary argues, adds botanical and ornithological ontologies to urban and architectural taxonomies of ruination. By positioning oneself in the disciplinary blur, the commentary ideates on how architectural and urban studies can accommodate unfamiliar rhythms of nonhuman-constructed botanical and ornithological ruins.

Urban Studies.title: Cultural buffering in entrepreneurial city diplomacy: Wuxi’s economic engagement abroad
Urban Studies.abstract: Why do investment-oriented municipal delegations begin with culture? This article develops cultural buffering to explain how municipal actors use cultural forms and assets when development-oriented diplomacy brings together organisations with different authority, timetables and commitments. The analysis draws on multi-sited ethnography of 5 Wuxi delegation circuits across Japan, the United Kingdom and continental Europe, followed by tracing of 21 initiatives to July 2026. It identifies two recurrent problems: municipal schedules can outrun partner learning and due diligence, while demands for visible outputs can exceed commitment and post-event ownership. Municipal actors respond to these temporal and accountability mismatches through naming, sequencing, coalition broadening and managed ambiguity. These moves can change who participates, what becomes discussable, which organisations enter the relationship and how provisional alignment is recorded. Subsequent project implementation depends on authority, resources, delivery capacity and an organisation willing to own the next step. Cultural buffering therefore identifies the encounter-level work through which an unsettled proposal becomes discussable and revisitable before its implementation is determined.

Environment and Planning A.title: Safe bonds, risky debt? Covered bonds and the financialisation of housing in Sweden
Environment and Planning A.abstract: Contributing to the literatures on housing financialisation and financial geography, this article examines the growth and role of covered bonds in fuelling housing financialisation in Sweden. Lauded as safer and more efficient alternatives to residential mortgage-backed securities, covered mortgage bonds – on-balance-sheet debt securities issued by banks to fund mortgages – provide investors with robust protection through dual recourse to both the issuing bank and the segregated ‘cover pool’ of mortgage assets. While the structure of these instruments provides a derisking function for bondholders, they simultaneously reconfigure the architecture of housing finance in permissive mortgage regimes, such as Sweden’s, by intensifying the supply of mortgage credit in highly leveraged urban centres and concentrating credit risk on the balance sheets of domestic banks. Drawing on the historiography of regulatory change, policy debates and interviews with stakeholders, the article investigates how, despite resistance from state authorities, Swedish finance lobbyists were able to successfully frame covered bond legislation as essential to maintaining international financial competitiveness. The Swedish case illustrates how the interplay between the structural power of domestic financial elites and European financial integration, mediated through national policy settings, reshapes housing and finance systems, deepening systemic interdependencies between the financial system, households and the state, while reconfiguring the geographies of financial risk.

Environment and Planning A.title: Financialization and Local Statecraft: Introduction to the book review forum
Environment and Planning A.abstract: This piece introduces a book review forum for Financialization and Local Statecraft by Andy Pike.

Environment and Planning A.title: Licensing liberal imperialism: The ‘rogue recruiter’ and the racial logic of low-wage labor supply chains
Environment and Planning A.abstract: Within much contemporary migration policy, labor recruiters are often understood as unscrupulous and state-evading actors embedded in informal networks of brokerage who profit from the demand for cheap labor abroad. To historians and other scholars of the British imperial indenture system, however, private labor recruiters of the late 19th century are understood as firmly situated within the imperial state’s apparatus of plantation labor recruitment and management. This paper seeks to bring analyses of scholars of indenture recruitment into closer conversation with critical migration scholarship on the contemporary regulation of labor recruiters in India. Drawing insights from these literatures together with archival data primarily on the 19th century Allahabad-Trinidad and indenture migration corridor which illuminates the structure and operation of indenture recruitment networks in the region that is present-day Uttar Pradesh, we examine the colonial repertoires of recruiter regulation that form the foundations of subcontracted recruitment networks in the region today. In particular, we foreground how two mechanisms of control and regulation—pyramid subcontracting and licensing—were vital in establishing a class of informalized, commission-based recruiters at the lowest tiers of the network. Drawing upon Denise Ferreira da Silva’s notion of the racial dialectic, we highlight the enduring use of licensing and subcontracting as a “colonial racial arsenal” which has always failed to effectively regulate recruiters and their networks. We foreground how, both then and now, these tools have instead served to delineate first-mile recruiters as racial rule-breaking subjects in an otherwise orderly and fair migration regime.

Environment and Planning A.title: When peripheral cities go viral: Platform interception, digital participation and the reconfiguration of city branding
Environment and Planning A.abstract: The rise of ‘internet-celebrity cities’ ( wanghong ) has become a new emblem of platform urbanism. Yet existing platform studies offer limited insight into this phenomenon as a product of digitally enabled city branding, an oversight that obscures the new dynamics that digital platforms introduce into entrepreneurial governance. To address this gap, this paper proposes a physical–virtual complementary framework for examining how platforms’ operations and local practices coalesce to (re)shape the image of cities. The framework is illustrated through a case study of Rongjiang , a peripheral Chinese city distinguished by its dramatic internet virality. In Rongjiang ’s digital branding endeavour, digital platforms reconfigured the composition, roles, and power dynamics of the stakeholders involved in city branding, extended the co-creation of city branding by enabling massive and unsupervised participation, and consolidated their own unbalanced control over selective online visibility. These findings highlight a paradox of digital empowerment in city branding: platforms enabled more extensive and decentralised branding participation while introducing and reinforcing a new, algorithm-dominated pattern of participation that redefined local agency in city branding. This research extends platform-urbanism scholarship beyond its predominantly economic and cultural discourses to engage with city branding as an integral part of the urban entrepreneurialism literature. The findings advance understanding of urban entrepreneurialism with particular attention to transforming local practices around plural participation in a platform-mediated urban age.

Environment and Planning A.title: Mombasa in the Second Cold War: Logistics polyalignment and the making of the gatekeeper city
Environment and Planning A.abstract: Over the past two decades, the city of Mombasa has undergone significant spatial transformations resulting from multiple large-scale infrastructure projects aimed at improving logistics efficiency along the Northern Economic Corridor (NEC). The Chinese-led Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) and the Japanese-led Mombasa Port Development Program (MPDP) particularly stand out due to their far-reaching effects on national and regional networks of commodity circulation. Although developed by competing powers and connected to rival connectivity agendas that unfold within the Second Cold War (CWII), their material integration drives urban change in Mombasa. This article analyzes the MPDP/SGR interface as manifesting Kenya’s logistics polyalignment—a mode of foreign engagement through which successive ruling coalitions leverage rival powers to produce transnationally oriented corridors and urban nodes. I demonstrate how, on the one hand, this mode of engagement plays out within a regional context shaped by geopolitical-economic rivalries over corridor centrality—a process that has gradually produced the NEC as materially polyaligned . On the other hand, I foreground how the material integration of projects connected to rival connectivity strategies in Mombasa has contingently transformed the city into a gatekeeper city . This urban form emerges as the MPDP/SGR nexus becomes a site of multiscalar power struggles over the circulation, distribution, and capture of value, where competing agendas advanced by rival state and non-state actors converge, with important implications for urban economies and livelihoods.

Environment and Planning B.title: AGORA cities: The hidden infrastructure shaping urban fragility
Environment and Planning B.abstract: Urban services are unevenly distributed across the city, yet it is unclear when their joint presence signals fragility and when it instead outlines a neighbourhood’s vocation. For Bologna and Florence, we integrate Foursquare and OpenStreetMap points of interest with Sentinel-2-derived green indicators based on the 3–30–300 rule, cluster urban areas accordingly, and benchmark the clusters against the demographic, social, economic, and composite fragility indices produced by the municipal statistical offices, which are exogenous to the analysis. In both cities, we identify a subset of infrastructures, termed AGORA (Arts, Green environments, and Open Routes for Access and mobility), whose joint provision is associated with lower fragility. The AGORA Alignment score (AA), based on the rank correlation between AGORA endowment and composite fragility, indicates full alignment in Florence (AA = 1.00) and strong but incomplete alignment in Bologna (AA = 0.80). The remaining service categories instead show wide and heterogeneous distributions: they differentiate areas without tracking fragility and can be interpreted as expressions of urban vocations. The least fragile cluster, the only one with full AGORA endowment, hosts just 3.3% of residents in Bologna and 6.3% in Florence. The framework offers a procedure transferable to other contexts and identifies the expansion of AGORA infrastructures as a candidate lever for reducing fragility without altering existing vocations.

Environment and Planning B.title: When does post-demolition vacancy become persistent, and how much vacant land remains? Nationwide evidence from South Korea
Environment and Planning B.abstract: Vacant-land inventories show where parcels remain vacant, but not how long they have remained without built reuse after demolition. Using nationwide administrative histories of 435,702 demolished parcels in South Korea (2005–2024), we link demolition dates to subsequent occupancy approvals and estimate Kaplan–Meier still-vacant curves. We identify when these curves enter a sustained period of slow decline, yielding two measures: stabilization time (ST), when the slowdown begins, and stabilization survival (SS), the share remaining without registered built reuse at that point. Under the main three-year persistence criterion, the pooled national curve reaches this phase 1055 days after demolition, with an estimated still-vacant share of 56.4%. Among parcels without observed registered built reuse at the end of 2024, 29% had elapsed durations shorter than this benchmark. Across 1148 neighborhoods, similar ST values can correspond to different SS values, and vice versa. Neighborhood and municipal conditions are more systematically associated with SS than with ST. These findings show that the timing of slowing reuse and the amount of vacancy remaining capture different aspects of post-demolition change.

Environment and Planning B.title: Predicting economies of scale in Brazilian municipal expenditure: Panel econometrics and interpretable machine learning
Environment and Planning B.abstract: Municipal size is a persistent question in urban planning and public finance because small jurisdictions may face high per capita costs, whereas larger jurisdictions may face congestion and administrative complexity. This study compares panel econometric and interpretable machine-learning models for real municipal operational expenditure per capita in Brazil. The analysis uses 49,228 municipality-year observations for 5,568 municipalities from 2013 to 2021 and evaluates prediction through municipality-holdout, temporal-holdout, and state-block designs. Histogram Gradient Boosting performs best for unseen municipalities and held-out states, while a municipality fixed-effects-style predictor performs best for later-year prediction of municipalities already observed in the panel. The results indicate strong economies of scale among small municipalities followed by a broad low-cost range rather than one universal optimum. Controlled econometric and spatial-error models imply minima near 143,000 to 176,000 residents, while a reduced-form pooled OLS model excluding grants implies about 232,000 residents. The strongest boosting models show no clear interior upturn within the evaluated grid, with predicted expenditure remaining within 10% of the minimum above approximately 48,000 to 53,000 residents. Grouped SHAP results rank population first, followed by grants and local economic capacity. Residual Moran tests show that unexplained expenditure differences remain spatially clustered. The findings support spatially informed expenditure benchmarking and caution against consolidation policies based on one fixed population threshold.

Environment and Planning B.title: Quantifying uncertainty in deep learning models for urban safety perception: An MC Dropout approach
Environment and Planning B.abstract: Deep learning models have revolutionized the automated analysis of urban perception. However, these models typically provide point predictions without associated uncertainty estimates, limiting their application in critical urban planning and policy decisions. This research explores the implementation of Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) as a method for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning models for urban safety perception. Using ResNet-based convolutional neural networks, we evaluated this approach on both global urban datasets (PlacePulse 2.0) and a specific case study of Santiago, Chile, focusing specifically on the safety dimension of urban perception. Our findings reveal that MC Dropout yields per-image uncertainty estimates without requiring significant architectural modifications, alongside a modest improvement in predictive accuracy (from 66.81% to 67.64%). We show that these estimates vary systematically with urban characteristics, with distinct patterns observed between different urban districts, and that the MC Dropout spread is systematically narrower than the discrepancy between the stochastic and deterministic predictions. We are explicit about what the study does not establish: none of our analyses tests the uncertainty estimates against predictive error, so we do not claim that they are calibrated or that they rank predictions by reliability, and we specify in detail the risk–coverage protocol and pairwise proper scoring rule that such a validation would require. The potential implications for urban analytics—triage of cases for human verification, mapping the spatial distribution of predictive dispersion within cities, and improved interpretability of model decision-making—are presented as prospective applications conditional on that validation. The methodological framework established here can be adopted and extended for future studies and practical applications in urban environments.

Environment and Planning B.title: Urban form typologies in Seoul since 1960: A framework for block-level classification and their changing prevalence over time
Environment and Planning B.abstract: This study proposes a framework for classifying urban form typologies at the block level and examining changes in their prevalence in Seoul since 1960. The study identifies major typologies aligned with urban planning trends and analyzes their morphological characteristics. Key questions addressed include: how many distinct urban form types can be identified in Seoul; what unique features define each type; and how changes in the prevalence of these types over time reflect broader urban development trends. The analytical procedure consisted of three steps. First, block units were defined based on infrastructure boundaries such as arterial roads. Second, eight indicators were established to capture the morphological features of blocks, parcels, streets, and buildings—the fundamental components of urban structure. Third, Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering was applied to classify blocks with similar numerical indicators into five distinct types. The result effectively captures how many morphological features aligned with Seoul’s urban planning objectives by era. Compared with previous typologies, the study integrates multiple scales of urban form and examines changes in typology prevalence across different periods, providing a basis for interpreting the historical process of urbanization.

Environment and Planning B.title: What defines the linear city? Examining accessibility premises with novel flow-based linearity indices
Environment and Planning B.abstract: This study re-examines the widely held assumption that the linear city model enhances both efficiency and equity of accessibility. From a space syntax perspective, we introduce two flow-based linearity indices: the Morphological Linearity Index, which captures how strongly path-implied trips align along a single axis, and the Structural Linearity Index, which captures how strongly paths converge on shared street segments. We then relate these indices to accessibility measures that are likewise derived from network configuration alone. Applying these indices to 60 South Korean cities, we find that corridor-centered structures alone do not guarantee efficient or equitable accessibility. Networks with higher morphological linearity show lower mean detour rates yet no corresponding reduction in average trip distance, a directness-distance trade-off that can offset net efficiency gains. Higher structural linearity is associated with both greater detour rates and longer trip distances, suggesting that corridor-centered designs can undermine overall accessibility. By translating the “linear city” into measurable indices, this study provides an operational basis for evidence-based road network planning and assessment.

Environment and Planning B.title: Generative AI for urban planning: Designing streetscapes from street-view imagery using diffusion models
Environment and Planning B.abstract: Street-view imagery (SVI) is widely used to quantify key indicators of urban environment, such as greenery, sky, or road view indices. However, relatively few studies have examined controlled SVI synthesis that combines explicit target proportions of trees, sky, buildings, and roads with road-layout masks, while also testing conflicts between textual and spatial controls. To address this gap, we propose a generative multimodal AI framework that synthesizes alternative streetscapes conditioned on targeted visual metrics, enabling direct visual exploration of urban scenarios. We first construct a multimodal dataset that aligns SVIs with textual descriptions, segmentation maps, road masks, and quantitative metrics of visual elements in Chicago and Orlando. Using this dataset, we demonstrate that diffusion models can produce realistic and semantically consistent streetscape imagery while responding to both textual and imagery controls. Our quantitative evaluations show that incorporating visual controls can improve semantic consistency, reducing the LPIPS index by approximately 6% while maintaining global visual realism. In addition, overall semantic consistency increases by 23.7% in Orlando and 46.4% in Chicago, as measured by the mIoU index, with class-wise gains exceeding 100% improvement for building view indices. Streetscape generation shows directional and interpretable responses to both visual and textual prompts, and when textual and visual controls conflict, imagery controls tend to dominate, indicating a clear control hierarchy and the importance of further developing visual controls for urban scene generation. Overall, this work establishes an important benchmark for streetscape generation using SVIs and diffusion models, and illustrates how generative AI can support controllable and exploratory urban scenario visualization.

Environment and Planning B.title: Assessing the association between street view–derived perceived liveliness and street thefts
Environment and Planning B.abstract: Crime geographers are attentive to how the spatial characteristics of the environment affect criminal behaviors. Recently, scholars have found that aside from physical and social attributes, the perception of the environment, such as safety perception, is also associated with crime occurrence. However, perceived liveliness, a visual perceptual proxy for potential routine activity settings that are closely linked to routine activity theory and crime pattern theory, is rarely explored in prior research. This study examines the association between perceived liveliness and street thefts in the City of Cincinnati, the United States. The liveliness perception scores are derived from street view imagery using a support vector machine model trained on the MIT Place Pulse V2 crowdsourcing image survey. Negative binomial regression models are used to test the relationships between perceived liveliness and street theft, with social and physical environmental attributes controlled. Results show that perceived liveliness significantly improves model performance and is positively associated with street theft. This study provides the first evidence that perceived liveliness helps explain crimes. The positive relationship between perceived liveliness of the built environment and crime adds a new dimension to the routine activity theory and the crime pattern theory. It also offers a scalable and cost-effective measure that can assist urban planners and law enforcement in identifying potential theft hotspots using readily available street view imagery.

Environment and Planning C.title: Surveilled bodies, normalized violence: Migrant women’s everyday experiences with digital-material surveillance in Singapore
Environment and Planning C.abstract: This paper examines how digital monitoring operates alongside face-to-face surveillance across socio-material-digital spaces, as contemporary migration to Singapore intersects with intensifying digital surveillance. Focusing on two non-elite, working-class groups of migrant women – migrant domestic workers and marriage migrants married to Singaporean men – we illustrate how entangled digital and non-digital surveillance practices produce gendered precarity through the mundane violence of everyday monitoring in both public and private spheres. We draw on qualitative interview and ethnographic data to demonstrate how surveillance reconfigures gendered boundaries of care and control while normalizing everyday violence against migrant bodies. Crucially, we reveal the ambivalent nature of surveillance as both a mechanism of control and a domain of migrant agency. Women experience and comply with surveillance to be seen as “good migrants,” while simultaneously engaging in lateral surveillance and reverse surveillance as tactics of negotiation and resistance. Ultimately, we argue that the normalization of hybrid surveillance conducts political work within Singapore’s constrained public spheres, producing working-class migrant women as active surveillance subjects whose sense of belonging remains deeply conditional.

Environment and Planning C.title: A climate of countering extremism? Exploring the enrolment of climate activism into UK counter-extremism policy discourses
Environment and Planning C.abstract: Climate activists are increasingly branded as ‘extremists’, ‘terrorists’, and ‘zealots’ by political actors hostile to decarbonisation, including the enrolment of climate activism into preventing/countering violent extremism (P/CVE) policies. Drawing inspiration from political geographic theorisations of territory ( Elden, 2010 ) and security ( Amoore, 2013 ), I conceptualise (counter-)extremism as a political technology which partially functions through the construction of spectrums (calculative discursive tools which take the form of an ‘array’ of possible positions). The paper draws on a discourse-historical analysis (DHA) and semi-structured interviews with activists based in the UK. I contend that two spectrums are constructed, each of which works according to a spatial logic: the first is an ideological spectrum, which positions climate activists as part of an extreme ‘far left’; and second is a spectrum of political practices which proximises physical violence to climate activists. I conclude with reflections on the implications of counter-extremism for climate activism, particularly in the context of the increasing repression of climate (and other) activists worldwide.

Environment and Planning C.title: On the intersection of Black geographies and policy mobilities: Tracing circuits of anti-racism in Newcastle upon Tyne
Environment and Planning C.abstract: This paper reflects theoretically on the intersection of Black geographies and policy mobilities by tracing the historical and contemporary movements of Black activists, intellectuals and anti-racist struggles in Newcastle upon Tyne. While Black geographies foregrounds Black spatial imaginaries, resistance and epistemologies rooted in racial capitalism and coloniality, it has insufficiently interrogated how racialized policy formations and their circulations function transjurisdictionally. Likewise, policy mobilities, which charts the movement and mutation of urban policy models across contexts, offers an opportunity to expose the racialized structures underpinning these movements. This paper develops a conceptual approach that examines how race and power circulate through circuits of racialized spatial practices, Black actors and political thought and anti-racist struggles. The paper traces how Black individuals, ideas and infrastructures – routed through historical visits by Martin Luther King Jr., Frederick Douglass and Muhammad Ali as well as through contemporary cultural programs like Freedom City and protest movements like Black Lives Matter – are mobilized within and beyond the urban. In so doing, it advances a global, relational understanding of Black spatial politics that provokes a rethinking of urban theory’s Euro-American biases.

Environment and Planning C.title: Branding cities or citizens? Virtue-based branding as a technology of subjectification in Louisville
Environment and Planning C.abstract: City branding is increasingly understood as shaping not only how cities are seen but who their residents become. This paper contributes to the growing scholarship that conceptualizes place branding as a technology of subjectification, arguing that when a city is branded with a human attribute, it is in effect its citizens who are branded. Drawing on a qualitative case study of Compassionate Louisville, the research traces how compassion was institutionalized as a governing discourse following the city’s formal adoption of the brand identity. The study reveals how the brand narrative operates simultaneously as a moral ideal, a performative expectation, and a political resource used to legitimize policy and manage social contradictions. By framing compassion as an apolitical, universal virtue, the brand establishes a disciplinary framework that encourages self-regulation and moral conformity while depoliticizing systemic social suffering. The paper contributes to debates within political geography and urban studies by demonstrating how virtue-based branding acts as an affective technology of power, reshaping urban subjectivities.

Environment and Planning C.title: The material infrastructure of privatization, dispossession and resistance at the Zambian land frontier
Environment and Planning C.abstract: The privatization of communal lands continues to be a central tenet of capitalist and settler-colonial appropriations with devastating implications for the dispossessed and land denied. This article traces how dispossession and resistance become bound up in the material infrastructure of privatization – fences, concrete, rebar and survey lines – and the colonial histories sedimented within them. In dialogue with legal-geographical work on property and materiality, I show how such artefacts become the nodes through which law’s abstraction gives way to struggle; once law is materialized in objects, these become susceptible to alteration and enrolment in new lives of legal association that can subvert – and creatively invert – the power trafficked through property. The analysis draws from ethnographic fieldwork in Mulonga village, central Zambia, where a privatization scheme evolved into a localized struggle between creative cultivators who reworked the things of property to resist displacement, and a bureaucracy that struggled to make them perform the political work assigned to them. Abstract property, I conclude, must be read alongside the contingency and resistant reworkings of its material articulation, which creates new legal surfaces upon which people can act, redirect legal signs, and unsettle translations through which private property achieves exclusionary effect.

Environment and Planning C.title: Saving lives or freeing territory? Sacred values and tragic trade-offs in wartime Ukraine
Environment and Planning C.abstract: President Zelensky has asserted: “We do not trade our lands and our people.” Both territorial integrity and human lives are considered ‘sacred values’ in wartime Ukraine, values beyond cost-benefit and exchange calculations. Yet, the human costs of continuing war to retake territory are so great in Ukraine that these sacred values are forced into a tragic trade-off. Using a survey of frontline Ukrainians from 2022 made up of residents and displaced persons equally (n = 1800), this paper shows that how the ‘lives versus territory’ dilemma divided respondents. We examined the degree to which wartime hatred of the Russian leadership and material insecurity explain people’s choices, and the role that personal stress plays as a mediator for these attitudes. The results reveal that respondents with higher levels of stress were more likely to prioritize saving lives over freeing territory. Displaced persons were also more likely to prioritize lives. The respondent’s material insecurity had modest impacts. For those most stressed during wartime, lives come before land.

Environment and Planning C.title: Walter Benjamin on natural history and place
Environment and Planning C.abstract: Taking his radio broadcast on the Mississippi flood of 1927 as a point of departure, this article argues that Walter Benjamin has much to contribute to current debates concerning space, nature, and place. Benjamin’s episode on the devastating flood in the American South was his final transmission for Berlin Radio’s Youth Hour in 1932, and it concludes a series of episodes on disasters that are both natural and social at once. This article situates the radio broadcast in relation to two catastrophic ways of seeing: first, in Benjamin’s work on the German mourning play , where the spatializing function of allegory transposes the temporal events of history into a spatial image, and second, in the weakly messianic vision of history as “one single catastrophe.” Drawing on these reorienting modes of vision, I argue that Benjamin’s curation of ancient and recent catastrophes across the world prompts his young listeners to recognize interlinked moments of danger spanning both historical time and global space.

Environment and Planning C.title: Producing spatial justice: Scalar governance and territorial differentiation in coastal China’s nuclear development
Environment and Planning C.abstract: Nuclear infrastructure development highlights an important empirical case in environmental governance: nuclear facilities concentrate environmental and social burdens locally, yet many projects proceed without sustained opposition. In the context of China, this paper argues that such outcomes are produced through county-level scalar governance strategies. Focusing on the Zhangzhou Nuclear Power Project, the study reconstructs how local authorities designed four concentric governance zones (20 km, 10 km, 2 km, 200 m) and calibrated distance-based interventions—compensation and relocation, tiered emergency planning and monitoring, graded communication and participation, and differentiated infrastructure and welfare investments—so that governance intensity corresponded to spatial exposure. Drawing on archival materials, policy documents, and semi-structured interviews with officials and project actors, corroborated by administrative records and implementation milestones, the analysis shows that scalar governance pursued distributive, procedural, and recognition objectives across zones. Importantly, the absence of organized resistance is interpreted not as conflict resolution but as the managed incorporation of grievances into institutional channels within a constrained political environment. By reframing nuclear legitimacy as the outcome of territorially differentiated state action, the paper contributes to debates on territory, scale, and environmental governance and positioning spatial justice as a conditional mechanism for managing uneven infrastructural risk.

Environment and Planning C.title: Contested spatialities of renewable energy expansion—Introduction to the theme issue
Environment and Planning C.abstract: Renewable energy increasingly complements fossil fuels in meeting rising global energy demand. Yet its rollout is neither even nor free of conflict. This theme issue foregrounds the spatialities and scales of renewable energy infrastructures and examines the deeply contested nature of energy transition efforts. Drawing on case studies from Morocco, Jordan, Namibia, Mexico, Brazil, Peru and Ecuador, the contributions offer insights into recent regional developments and highlight transregional and cross-scalar interrelations. They connect place-based research on contested energy projects in political ecology, geography and anthropology with nation-focused analyses of energy transition policy, and approach scale as an unfolding field of contestation. In doing so, they challenge notions of a homogeneous “local” in analyses of energy conflict and move beyond methodological nationalism while still recognizing the significance of the national scale. Together, the theme issue demonstrates the value of relational approaches for disentangling and understanding the contested geographies of contemporary renewable energy expansion.
