Progress in Human Geography.title: Geographies of production I: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence
Progress in Human Geography.abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly shaped the landscapes of production since the early 2020s. This report reviews the scholarly debate on geographies of production and includes further developments in the spatiality of digitalisation. It draws on literature on firms that develop and offer AI as a product innovation (geographies of production of AI) and firms that implement and use AI (geographies of production with AI). The report highlights current trends, reveals research gaps, and finally addresses some implications for public debate.

Progress in Human Geography.title: Towards a new age of renting: Reimagining housing geographies beyond generation rent
Progress in Human Geography.abstract: This paper critically reviews post-2008 housing geographies while reframing the field around the socio-spatial implications and possibilities of enduring housing insecurity. I introduce the new age of renting as a politico-economic conjuncture and demographic shift marked by an ageing and increasingly heterogeneous renter population. Against the logics of homeownership ideology, family-mediated asset-based welfare, and the digital governance of rental markets, I examine trajectories obscured by the generation rent framing as a window onto unfolding, though not inevitable, precarious futures. From this vantage point, I explore how changes in tenants’ social composition create possibilities to challenge housing structures and reimagine futures.

Progress in Human Geography.title: Psychedelic geographies
Progress in Human Geography.abstract: This paper introduces psychedelic geographies as micropolitical praxis for unsettling the spatiotemporal closures of colonial capitalism, and enlivening alternative ways of being in the present. Building from Indigenous practices, countercultural histories, and the contemporary ‘psychedelic renaissance’, the paper argues that psychedelic geographies, in conjunction with (but distinct from) other radical geographical literatures, can provide important interjection into debates about how radically different experiences of space are experienced and prefigurative. Psychedelic geographies are situated alongside literatures on affect, hauntology, pluriverse imaginaries, and quantum geographies, not to supplant them but to bring them into productive resonance critiquing capitalistic spatial and temporal logics.

Progress in Human Geography.title: Abolitionist feminist geography: A framework for investigating the spatial dimensions of carceral reproductive injustice
Progress in Human Geography.abstract: Carceral spaces and practices threaten the reproductive rights of women and gender diverse people. As the global population of people in prisons for women is growing, there is a need for research exploring how the spaces and practices of detainment produce reproductive injustice. This article provides an overview of existing geographic and reproductive justice scholarship within the context of incarceration and reproductive rights, identifies potential convergences between reproductive justice theory and fields of abolition and carceral geography, and proposes a research agenda of abolitionist feminist geography to guide inquiry into the experience of carceral spaces as sites of reproductive injustice.

Progress in Human Geography.title: Tourism geography I: Capitalist accumulation and the socioecological limits of tourism
Progress in Human Geography.abstract: Over the past two decades, tourism geographers have approached tourism as a mode of capitalist accumulation that produces space, reorganizes labor and social reproduction, and appropriates nature. This report traces that shift through work on uneven development, financialization, platform capitalism, labor, and political ecology. It distinguishes limits to growth from the contradictions and limits generated through accumulation. These tensions become visible in debates over overtourism, while degrowth, post-capitalist, and regenerative approaches ask what contraction, redistribution, and ecological repair might require. I argue that tourism offers human geography a critical vantage point for examining how these relations might be organized otherwise.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: Animals’ territories
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual framework for research on animals’ territories. It starts from a genealogy of the fraught traffic of territorial ideas between ethology and geography, in which the disavowal of biological determinism led to a stark humanist divide in territorial research in political geography. It argues that this division is founded on an anachronistic understanding of animal behaviour, which hinders the development of a more-than-human conception of territory in political geography, ultimately limiting critical analysis of the widespread and often devastating human impacts on animals’ territories. To redress these problems, the second and third sections draw on recent ethological research to introduce animals’ terrain – defined as the material properties of a territory sensed in relation to animals’ Umwelten – and animals’ territorialities or territorial practices. It shows how analyses of animals help further calls for plural and material accounts of territory. A fourth section outlines and evaluates a model of territory for a practical politics of multispecies coexistence premised on wild diplomacy through interspecies communication. The conclusions identify key points for dialogue with both animal and political geographers. The analysis is illustrated with examples of the territorial birds and mammals that predominate in research in ethology and animal geography.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: Cartographies of sacrifice: Mnemonic geography, martyr commemoration and the making of national space in palestine
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This article theorizes Nablus, a Palestinian city in the contemporary West Bank, as a cultural geographic site that exemplifies a rich cartography of sacrifice wherein urban spaces become inseparable from memory and identity. Drawing on Palestinian scholarship on memory, spatial practice and everyday life, we argue that the Old City of Nablus functions as a counter-geography in which martyr memory, survival and belonging are continually inscribed and lived. Its memorial walls and improvised shrines operate as mnemonic devices and spatial archives that reflect a long history of collective loss and resilience. Space is often weaponized in Palestine: checkpoints disrupt continuity, surveillance causes anxiety and settlements continue to radically change topography. However, in Nablus, ṣumūd or steadfastness allows people to reclaim their city and reconstruct its national value by turning geography into a narrative of commemoration. Drawing on interviews with residents and analysis of graffiti, heritage signs and commemorative sites in Nablus's Old City (al-Balda al-Qadīma), we suggest that memory is actively performed when mourning is intertwined with everyday life, thereby materializing a living geography of sacrifice and endurance. The article concludes that Nablus is an enduring testimony to how Palestinian urban spaces resist erasure by transforming martyrdom into a spatial language that embodies persistence.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: On hinterlands
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: Rosen and Alvarez León's typology of “variegated hinterlands” provides a powerful and timely analytic for examining digital capitalism. This commentary pushes the authors on two fronts: first, I question the fluidity between types of hinterlands and their related cores, warning against a typological collapse in which all spaces become hinterlands to some other; second, I push the authors to further define the differences in kind from previous iterations of capitalist expansion and exploitation. To do so, I highlight the growing computational inversion in which data is extracted from urban cores to be processed, analyzed, and decided upon by algorithmic agents located in distant, traditionally defined hinterlands. To better understand this inversion and its already-arriving impacts, I argue geographers must use the typology not simply to map the traces of these relations, but to build a topology of contestation.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: Volumetric commensuration and its remainders
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This commentary responds to Daniel Paiva's call for the right to atmosphere by advancing the framework of following air rights . I treat breathable air, buildable volume and emission allowances as claims held apart by three interrelated operations: differentiation, detachment and conversion. Comparing two instruments, I argue that the property/commons contradiction is produced by design and not just given in nature. Admissibility – whether claims are admitted for political consideration – is a prior condition of meaningful participation.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: Planetary 'Singaporeanization': Geopolitics within planetary rural/urban geographies
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This commentary engages the article by Chi-Mao Wang, Damien Maye, and Michael Woods (2025) on ‘Planetary rural geographies’ through the vantage point of the city-state of Singapore. We argue that viewing the themes developed by Wang et al. from and through Singapore and other city-states brings out (geo)political frames – notably sovereignty, empires, and their aftermaths – with implications for other cases, sites, and the wider conceptual debate.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: Atmospheric fury, shadows of agonism, and the ethics of abolishing worlds
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This commentary engages Daniel Paiva’s (2026) proposal to think the ‘right to atmosphere’ in agonistic terms. First, drawing on Michel Serres, it elaborates the role of turbulent ‘fury’ in the elemental constitution of atmospheres. It argues the fury fundamentally troubles agonistic pluralism by showing how worlds are broken, ended and produced through materialities that do not easily lend themselves to what remains central to the ‘right to atmosphere’. After looking at the collective equivalence of fury, the commentary turns, second, to the three shadows of agonism – intrinsic atmospheric seductions, unruly movements irreducible to identifiable origins or parties to a conflict, and brutal colonial shadows shattering the promises of productive conflict – problematising the assumption that conflict necessarily functions as a creative, productive and capacitating force. Finally, drawing on abolitionist thought, it asks whether the solution to unequal access to atmospheres, one capable of acknowledging the anti-oppressive ethics of care underlined by Paiva, is inclusion and participation, or the abolition of oppressive worlds.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: LGBTphobia as a multiscale assemblage: Rural LBT women’s everyday geographies
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This article examines LGBTphobia as experienced by lesbian, bisexual, and transgender (LBT) women in Israeli rural space. Conceptualized here as a multiscale assemblage, five manifestations of LGBTphobia are presented: (1) Whispering, giggling and gossip; (2) insults related to sexual and gender identity; (3) discrimination and exclusion; (4) intrusion, sexualization, and eroticization; and (5) Condescension and boundary construction. Although neoliberal discourses often assume that LGBTQ + acceptance has become increasingly widespread, particularly in urban settings, this analysis demonstrates that inclusion does not eliminate LGBTphobia. Rather, inclusion and LGBTphobia coexist, with narratives of progress and acceptance frequently obscuring more subtle yet persistent forms of exclusion, marginalization, and prejudice. Relatedly, whereas recent scholarship suggests that rural areas may serve as spaces of tolerance and safety for LGBTQ + s thanks to the diffusion of urban discourses of acceptance into rural contexts, the findings show how LGBTphobia becomes internalized, embodied, and affectively reproduced in everyday life. Among LBT women interviewed, the anticipation of LGBTphobia prompted self-censorship even before any overt incidents occurred. These dynamics reveal LGBTphobia as an embodied and spatial structure rather than a solely interpersonal phenomenon, continuing to shape participants’ everyday rural lives despite apparent social progress.

Dialogues in Human Geography.title: Layered proximity: Distant time and deferred temporality in circular bioeconomy
Dialogues in Human Geography.abstract: This commentary engages Datta's concept of distant time, which explains how colonial statecraft governs subaltern populations through temporal deferral, keeping them suspended in conditions of waiting while framing displacement and demolition as development. Building on Datta's work, I argue that her framework under-theorizes the complementary process of temporal compression. Using Harvey's concept of time-space compression as a conceptual lens and drawing on scholarship on the circular bioeconomy, I show how contemporary colonial-capitalist governance not only defers justice but also compresses marginalized communities into global circuits of value in real time. In the circular bioeconomy, forests, farmers, and waste pickers are rendered immediately governable and economically productive, even as the benefits they help generate are projected into an indefinitely deferred future. Rather than replacing Datta's framework, I propose a reorientation toward a theory of layered proximity, where immediate material incorporation coexists with the continuous postponement of justice.

Antipode.title:
An Academic Space of Radical Care and Orientation Towards African Urban Praxis: The Story of
                    UTA
                    ‐Do
Antipode.abstract: Marginalised academics have wandered off and created spaces to sustain each other in the racialised ecosystem that is the academy. In this paper, I use autoethnographic experience, workshop immersion and detailed analysis of relationships among participants of the Urban Theory Africa Doing (UTA‐Do) workshop to show the liberatory potential of spaces created in the margins by marginalised academics. UTA‐Do is an annual, week‐long workshop that brings together scholars, activists and practitioners working on African Urbanism and has been held in Eastern Africa for 4 years. Through its story, I argue that such spaces nurture liberatory practices of radical care that become instrumental to participants' navigation of the academy. Secondly, building on Sara Ahmed's concept of orientations, I argue that such gatherings are grounding in that they orient participants towards particular directions. In the case of UTA‐Do, I argue that it has been grounding UTA‐Do(ers) towards situated African urban research praxis.

Antipode.title: Theorizing Racisms Across Italy and the United States: Lessons From Gramsci and Du Bois
Antipode.abstract: The 2020 Italian Black Lives Matter mobilizations were a powerful incitement to consider what is at stake in understanding Italy as part of the global history of racial capitalism—and resistance against it. To do this, it is urgent for scholars to move from comparative to relational approaches in the study of global racisms. I argue that Antonio Gramsci and W.E.B. Du Bois provide a powerful set of analytical tools for breaking out of methodological nationalism in the study of racism and race in Italy—and beyond. When read together, Gramsci's writings on Italian national unification and Du Bois' writings on post‐Civil War Reconstruction in the United States offer both a historical grounding for understanding the connections between contestations over race and nation in Italy the United States, and a framework for how to think relationally about struggles against racism and fascism unfolding in both countries today.

Antipode.title: Reproducing Water Coloniality: Water Switching and State‐Backed Accumulation by Dispossession in Mauritius
Antipode.abstract: This article brings to light the coloniality of water in Mauritius—the ways in which colonially inherited water resource allocations continue to shape contemporary power relations underpinning elite accumulation by dispossession. It conceptualises ‘water switching’, the redirection of water to ever new profitable uses, as the process enabling continuous accumulation and reproducing coloniality. These dynamics rely on an active, enabling state. By generating an original typology of state support mechanisms—coercion, legitimisation, facilitation—the paper offers a framework for analysing the politics of dispossession. State‐capital symbiosis explains why these mechanisms persist, showing how Mauritius' economic development and the state's own legitimacy are deeply entwined with the protection of inherited elite privilege. The paper concludes by showing how the Mauritian case provides a basis for examining the role of resource endowments enabling accumulation across other sectors and geographies.

Antipode.title: Karachi in/and Sindh: Articulations, Disarticulations and the Eternal Reciprocity of Tears
Antipode.abstract: This paper develops a Gramscian sensitivity towards spatial claims and popular imaginaries to explore intertwined urban and national questions in Pakistan. The relationship between Karachi, Pakistan's largest city, and wider Sindh province animates intense contestation. Post‐1970s, this generated exclusivist ethnic politics, mediated through reified spatial divisions and claims over city, urbanity and nation. By analysing cultural and political productions, this paper considers shifting registers of urbanity, land and nation in the present conjuncture of crisis and dispossession. It delineates different articulations of urban and national questions, their slippages and contradictions, with an eye towards more inclusive, people‐centred resolutions of the Karachi–Sindh relationship. Drawing on Gramsci, the paper foregrounds the constitutive role of spatial imaginaries and practices in forging hegemonic projects. It thus calls attention to the situated spatial claims (including over city, urbanity and nation) produced by processes of urbanization and dispossession and the responsibility of intellectual‐cultural productions therein.

Antipode.title: The Limits of Cash: Guaranteed Income, Basic Income, and the Reproduction of the Precarious City
Antipode.abstract: Guaranteed income pilots and COVID‐era relief payments share a political form: they are time‐limited. This paper asks what that form does in a racialized housing market undergoing restructuring. Drawing on a five‐year participatory panel study of low‐income, predominantly Black women in Preservation of Affordable Housing properties in Cincinnati's Over‐the‐Rhine, we find that a bounded infusion of unconditional cash left the distributive register unmoved while the relational one eroded around it. Within‐person, neighborhood attachment declined significantly over the payment period and did not recover; social cohesion held through the infusion and then fell sharply after it ended; financial strain moved in neither direction. We read the pattern as normalization, a governing technology that holds precarity within a manageable range through statutory sunsets, tax‐credit covenants, and a resumed eviction docket. The argument is not against cash but against the assumption that a distributive instrument can reach a relational injury.

Antipode.title: Hidden Fractures: Communal Capitalist Urban Transformation in Post‐Protest Delhi
Antipode.abstract: This paper examines how the 2019–2020 Shaheen Bagh protests in Delhi, a landmark movement against India's Citizenship Amendment Act, accelerated urban transformations that extend well beyond the protest site. Drawing on ten months of comparative ethnographic fieldwork (2022–2023) in Shaheen Bagh, Jaitpur and Jasola Vihar, the study shows how communal capitalism, a mode of rule in which Hindu nationalist domination directs capitalist development, reshaped urban space and social relations in the protest's aftermath. The paper reads the post‐protest period through a Foucauldian account of visibility and discipline joined to the Symposium's concept of communal capitalism: the knowledge produced about a ‘dangerous’ neighbourhood becomes the basis both for its containment and for the value extracted from it. First, it shows how an initial show of sovereign force was joined by pervasive forms of control, including heightened state surveillance and community self‐regulation. Second, it traces how the exclusion of Muslims was made productive, with paradoxical results: while offering new economic opportunities to some Muslims, these dynamics also deepen spatial segregation and internal stratification. Third, it follows these processes across three localities, whose different patterns are shaped by class composition, property relations and histories of communal interaction. The findings contribute to debates on authoritarian urbanism, on Muslim urban experiences in contemporary India and on communal capitalism. The paper argues that moments of political resistance may accelerate patterns of spatial segregation while spurring new forms of economic and social adaptation in marginalised communities.

Antipode.title: Black and Pan‐African Joy and the Specter of Fascism
Antipode.abstract: This paper situates contemporary neofascism within the history of racial capitalism, arguing that Black Joy and “Emancipation Circuits” constitute material practices of resistance to dehumanization. Grounding capitalist transformations in the systematic negation of Black humanity, it challenges abstract accounts of valorization and explores joy's ontological foundations in African traditions of optimism and collective struggle. It critiques Eurocentric interpretations of Nazism and fascist terror, examining how Cold War deployments of authoritarianism obscured the historical relations through which fascism emerged and consolidated. It identifies sonic landscapes, from jazz to R&B, as “rival geographies” of autonomous expression and resistance. Contrasting Wagnerian aesthetic closure with John Coltrane's improvisational freedom, it locates Black music within emancipation struggles. Finally, it advocates a “popular multiracial front from below” uniting anti‐racist, feminist, and Indigenous struggles against the normalization of financial warfare and the deployment of technological force that facilitate the maturation of neofascism into fully consolidated fascist rule.

Antipode.title: Governing the Future: Artificial Intelligence as an Anticipatory Infrastructure of Control
Antipode.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in systems of governance, yet its political implications remain insufficiently theorized. This paper argues that AI is best understood as an anticipatory infrastructure of control: a form of power that operates through the preemptive governance of possible futures. Drawing on cases of biometric border systems, predictive policing, and AI‐enabled surveillance in authoritarian contexts, it shows how algorithmic systems classify and intervene on the basis of predicted risk. In doing so, they shift governance from regulating past and present conduct to managing future possibilities. Extending theories of discipline, biopolitics, and control, the paper demonstrates how anticipatory control is unevenly distributed, disproportionately targeting migrants, racialized communities, and political dissidents within longer histories of colonial domination and social inequality. Addressing these dynamics requires moving beyond the regulation of technologies to contesting the infrastructures through which futures are governed.

Antipode.title: Epistemic Civic Death: Knowledge Infrastructures, Disciplinary Hegemony, and the Destruction of Critical Geographies
Antipode.abstract: Accounts of authoritarian assault on universities center the scholar: dismissed, detained, exiled, reduced to civic death. This paper moves from the knower to the conditions of knowing. I call their destruction epistemic civic death : the dismantling of infrastructures that make critical knowledge collectively possible, such as platforms, pedagogies, and networks of trust and citation. It addresses a blind spot across academic freedom, geographies of knowledge, and comparative authoritarianism. Reading Foucault and Gramsci through Mbembe, I trace a disciplinary necropolitics where the state supplies the instrument of exception and a hegemonic discipline the target. My case is Turkish geography, built to serve a national imaginary and silent on class, ethnicity, and gender. The critical knowledge infrastructure built around the Turkish Association of Geographers was dissolved by emergency decree in 2016. I write from inside that closure. The association reopened in 2018; the community did not. An administrative decision can restore an institution, not the infrastructure of knowing it sustained.

Antipode.title: The Afterlives of Homeland: Black Veteran Homelessness and Racial Geographies of Unbelonging
Antipode.abstract: This article examines how Black veterans experiencing homelessness navigate the racialized geographies of “homeland” in the United States. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork with Walter (pseudonym), a 65‐year‐old Black Vietnam veteran living unhoused in Boulder, Colorado, I argue that the US homeland emerges in his experience as a racialized field of continual displacement. Walter's everyday life reveals a dissonance between the homeland's promise of security and his growing loss of faith in the institutions charged with providing care and protection. Bringing Black Geographies into conversation with scholarship on homeland security and homelessness, the article traces how Walter's memories of anti‐Black violence in Mississippi and Vietnam, his refusal to engage with the Department of Veterans Affairs, and his reliance on a fragile power wheelchair illuminate what I conceptualize as racialized homeland insecurity. His humor and reflections on survival also reveal forms of Black spatial knowledge through which he insists on living otherwise.

IJURR.title:
GENTRIFYING CAPITAL FROM WITHIN
                    : Rethinking Transnational Gentrification, Spatial Fix and Transnational Migration through Foreign, Urban and Rural Circuits in Kumasi, Ghana
IJURR.abstract: In this article, we examine the rapid neighbourhood transformation of Ahodwo in Kumasi, Ghana, where Chinese entrepreneurial migrants have settled over two decades. We draw on qualitative fieldwork to advance arguments that extend the concepts of transnational gentrification, spatial fix, and transnational migration, and demonstrate that the capital driving neighbourhood change in Ahodwo operates through two intersecting circuits: a transnational one, involving the direct investment of Chinese surplus capital in urban businesses, and a domestic one, where profits from informal gold mining (galamsey) in rural and periurban areas are reinvested into urban businesses. This insight deviates from the assumption that transnational gentrification is primarily financed from overseas and brings into view rural–urban capital circuits within the global South. Gentrifying capital is therefore both exogenous and endogenous, interacting in complex ways. The process is also locally curated: local landlords and brokers facilitate the clustering of a foreign tenant class by tailoring commercial and residential spaces, financing neighbourhood security, and producing conditions for a transnational rent gap. These dynamics inflate rents, reprofile tenants, and generate varied displacement forms. Chinese migration in Ahodwo uniquely coproduces capital and urban transformation across foreign, urban, and rural settings, challenging conventional narratives of capital origins, circulation, and gentrification.

IJURR.title:
TERRITORIAL VALORIZATION
                    : How Positive Stereotypes Advance Suburban Water Insecurity in Detroit
IJURR.abstract: Suburbs historically enabled and protected white middle‐class wealth in the United States; however, their more recent diversification has included a rise in suburban poverty. This article examines these dynamics through the issue of household water access—a feature of rising suburban impoverishment that deserves greater attention. For two years, the first author participated in a Detroit‐area advocacy group, working together to conduct interviews with a hard‐to‐reach group of suburban residents struggling to afford their water bills. These 15 interviews reveal that water insecurity affects households even in the most affluent suburbs and that access to water assistance and affordability programs has been inadequate and variable. We explain these findings by developing the concept of territorial valorization —the relational counterpart of territorial stigma—to capture the phenomenon whereby certain areas may fail to acknowledge and address social problems in an effort to maintain their historically positive reputations. While territorial valorization has the power to attract investment and resources, we theorize that its positive stereotypes can have negative consequences for residents who fail to meet their demands.

IJURR.title:
HOUSING RETROFITS IN JUST TRANSITIONS
                    ? Emerging Contradictions in Catalonia, Spain
IJURR.abstract: Efforts to decarbonize residential housing are growing globally. Following ambitious targets set by the European Commission's Renovation Wave and subsidized through Covid‐19 recovery funds, Spain's housing retrofit programme deployed EUR 3.4 billion in European grants to retrofit half a million homes between 2022 and 2026. This article uncovers emerging political, economic, environmental and social contradictions around expanding housing retrofits in Spain, with a focus on Catalonia, to explore how funds were disbursed and who stands to benefit. In considering the political economy of housing in just transitions, I draw from two dozen interviews in 2023 with a range of actors, meeting observations and grey literature to highlight contradictions emerging across five domains. These include the territorial distribution of funds, the universal nature of retrofit grants, the treatment of vulnerable populations, the scale of intervention and the nature of the housing retrofit sector. Together the contradictions largely illustrate how public retrofit funding has favoured increased capital circulation alongside reinforced social relations and ideologies of private property ownership and wealth accumulation. While the overall push is towards what I term a Spanish growth economy of housing repair, some contradictions in the five domains point to possibilities for a more transformative just housing transition.

IJURR.title:
NAVIGATING UNCERTAINTY IN REGIONAL SOFT PLANNING
                    : The Interpretive Dynamics of Emerging Planning Practices
IJURR.abstract: This study investigates how uncertainty shapes the emergence and implementation of a new regional soft planning practice. While soft, non‐statutory planning has been widely discussed, less is known about how actors interpret these new regional planning practices and how uncertainty persists beyond formal adoption. The article addresses this gap by conceptualizing uncertainty as foundational, relational and temporal, and examining how these dimensions structure collaboration between a regional authority and its municipalities. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with municipal and regional planners in Region Östergötland in Sweden, the analysis shows how unclear starting conditions and institutional ambiguity made it difficult for actors to understand the purpose and implications of the new regional planning practice. We demonstrate how uneven capacities between large and small municipalities translated interpretive openness into asymmetrical influence at first, how uncertainty was consciously used as a deliberate tactic to allow for more open discussions, and how uncertainty endured after adoption as actors struggled to relate the non‐binding strategy to statutory planning instruments and implementation responsibilities. We argue that uncertainty is not only a hindrance but a constitutive feature of regional soft planning, simultaneously enabling experimentation and risking reinforcing power asymmetries.

IJURR.title:
EMIGRE CITY
                    ‐
                    MAKING
                    : The Micropolitics of Diasporic Real Estate Investment and Urban Growth in Pakistan
IJURR.abstract: Contemporary cities in the global South are being reshaped through the intersecting logics of burgeoning real estate sectors and diasporic investment. This article examines the case of Pakistan to explore how emigration trajectories and remittance practices contribute to the transformation of urban landscapes in countries of origin through processes of emigre city‐making. Over the past few decades, the neoliberalizing real estate sector has aligned with shifts in the investment practices of elite emigrants, redirecting remittances from home‐building—once intended for eventual return—to speculative investments in urban real estate. These investments are part of broader, multi‐sited transnational strategies aimed at supporting permanent settlement in North Atlantic countries. Often made during presales, these speculative purchases and accompanying risk‐mitigation strategies help to create a niche market for vacant land, particularly in developments led by the military and its allies. These investments contribute to urbanization in major, second‐tier and emerging cities through low density suburban gated communities. By tracing the logics of such investments, this article sheds light on alternative trajectories of transnational urbanism and neoliberalization, illustrating how land and housing financialization unfolds in postcolonial cities through global flows of non‐corporate private capital, rather than institutional transnational capital and well‐developed financial markets.

IJURR.title:
NEGATIVE ASSETS
                    : Settler Colonialism, Speculative Urbanism, and the Moral Economy of Smallholding on Nairobi's Real Estate Frontier
IJURR.abstract: The expansion of Nairobi's real estate frontier into its peri‐urban hinterlands creates new opportunities and new dilemmas for smallholder families whose land is skyrocketing in value. Instead of taking the opportunity to become urban rentiers, many smallholders across Nairobi's peripheries are selling their inherited ‘ancestral’ plots in spite of strident taboos about the dangers of alienating patrimonial property. To explain why this is the case, we demonstrate how settler colonial histories of land reform created a demographic of smallholders that possessed land as a ‘negative asset’, never viable for long‐term commercial farming, and to which they became precariously rooted. While land's status as a commodity has been resisted despite titling, its rising value suggests that the commodification process is approaching thorough completion, with meagre plots sold rather than retained. Drawing on ethnographic cases of land sale, the article argues that the combination of settler colonial histories of land reform and the arrival of the real estate frontier works together to erode the moral economy of smallholding, forcing ‘ancestral’ land onto the market.

IJURR.title:
SPACE AND POLITICAL PARTICIPATION IN POPULAR NEIGHBORHOODS
                    : Insights from the Chilean Urban Uprising
IJURR.abstract: In this article we examine how space shapes the political dispositions of residents in marginalized neighborhoods and gave form to institutional and contentious participation during the 2019 urban uprising in Chile. Based on qualitative research in two neighborhoods on Santiago's outskirts, we reconstruct residents’ engagement with politics prior to and during the urban uprising. We use Lefebvre's relational concept of space in dialogue with Bourdieu's theory of habitus to understand how space (perceived, conceived, lived) interacts with individual resources, mainly cultural capital. This interaction shows that participation strategies during the revolt stemmed from political dispositions developed over time, having been shaped by the diverse and conflicting ways residents perceive, conceive, and live space. These strategies are also influenced by what Bourdieu terms residents’ ‘volume of capital’. Based on their political dispositions, residents of popular neighborhoods display a varied repertoire of political strategies. These strategies include institutional, collaborative, and oppositional participation, with the aim of resolving their daily material needs, affecting national politics, and challenging the neighborhood's reputation within the city's imagination.

IJURR.title:
‘
                    PARTICIPATION IS WHAT WE DO EVERY DAY
                    ’: Unpacking the Meanings and Practices of Participation Addressing Mobility Justice in Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre, Brazil
IJURR.abstract: Participation is a topic that has been widely debated in urban studies. Despite this, we argue in this paper that policies and academic work on mobility planning have paid little attention to the meanings attached to participation and its role in mobility justice. Building on the literature on spaces for participation, Southern theories and insurgent planning, this paper shows that participation has multiple and contested meanings, particularly when addressing mobility injustices in the global South. Based on case studies in Favela Santa Marta, Rio de Janeiro, and Vila Tronco, Porto Alegre, both in Brazil, we provide evidence of alternative meanings of participation and a range of participatory practices exercised by residents with, despite, and against the state. The everyday practices that flow from and interact with these meanings uphold the freedoms to move around, thrive, and dwell, challenging mobility planning and what we call ‘authorized participatory discourse’. Our findings show that while participation with the state is only one part of the story, particularly in contexts of informality and exclusion, the state's and residents’ responses are far from monolithic. We conclude by arguing that a focus on everyday practices can add new insights to the understanding of mobility justice and insurgent planning.
